claims.text: Standard zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding has a native oxide layer.
An ultra-thin, nano-engineered Al2O3 coating can be deposited on zirconium-alloy cladding by controlled chemical vapor deposition or a similar technique.
The intervention will produce a dense, continuous, and well-adhered Al2O3 surface layer.
The Al2O3 layer acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
The Al2O3 layer limits oxygen ingress into the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Reducing oxygen flux to the substrate slows elevated-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Slower oxidation kinetics reduce oxide growth and subsequent cladding degradation.
Al2O3-coated zirconium-alloy cladding will oxidize more slowly than uncoated cladding during otherwise identical high-temperature steam exposure.
The coating will delay the onset of rapid oxidation relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding.
After the same high-temperature exposure period, coated cladding will have lower weight gain than uncoated cladding.
After the same high-temperature exposure period, coated cladding will have a thinner oxide layer than uncoated cladding.
The coating will retain the cladding's suitability for reactor service.
The oxidation-resistance benefit depends on the alumina coating maintaining adhesion and integrity during thermal cycling and typical reactor operating stresses.
Coating degradation or spallation would eliminate the proposed oxidation-resistance benefit.
Cyclic thermal loading and irradiation may reduce the coating's adhesion and protective performance during long-term reactor service.
The proposed benefit is expected during steam exposure above 700°C.

contradictions.description: The conditions combine steam exposure above 700°C representing severe operational or accident scenarios with the requirement to retain 'normal reactor operating conditions'; these are distinct exposure regimes and are not coherently reconciled.

The boundary makes coating integrity a precondition for the hypothesis, whereas the falsification rule treats coating degradation itself as falsification. Under a strictly conditional claim, failure of the stated precondition would place the test outside the claimed domain rather than falsify performance when the coating remains intact.
